You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Costco Q4 Earnings Preview: Membership and Capital-Return Test After a Near-Bear Pullback

TEXT:
🔥 US Stock Hotspot Radar is Live! Content: 3 major themes + 6 selected stocks + 7 key events. Where are this week’s opportunities? Click the link to see all 22 trading directions in one chart →
Investment Snapshot
Costco (COST.US) will report fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results (16-week period ended August 30) after the U.S. close on September 24, 2026. Wall Street consensus looks for total revenue of about $94.8 billion (about +10.0% YoY) and adjusted EPS of about $6.53 (about +11.2% YoY versus $5.87 a year earlier). Full-year EPS is expected near $20.5 (versus about $18.2 last year), with annual revenue potentially topping $301 billion.
The company has already printed Q4 net sales of $93.9 billion (+11.3% YoY), with comparable sales +9.4% and +6.7% excluding gasoline and FX. The debate is therefore not whether Costco sold merchandise, but whether membership-fee quality, margins, tariff-refund reinvestment, and a possible special dividend or buyback can reset the tape. Shares have fallen about 18% from the May high of $1,096.50 to a September 22 close of $899.41. Valuation digestion and the earnings print arrive together.
Four Things That Matter
Focus 1: Can the membership flywheel offset slower traffic?
Costco’s profit engine is membership fees, not merchandise markup. Q3 membership-fee income was $1.37 billion (+10.7% YoY, about +9.9% YoY ex-FX). Paid members reached 82.9 million (+4.1% YoY) and Executive members 41.2 million (+9.6% YoY). Renewal rates were 92.2% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.7% worldwide. Q4 needs to show that renewals are holding, Executive mix is still rising, and digital acquisition is not quietly impairing future renewal rates. Soft membership metrics would invite a re-rating from “premium retailer” to “mature retailer.”
Focus 2: Comps are already out; margins decide the beat
The top line is largely locked in: Q4 net sales $93.9 billion (+11.3% YoY), U.S. comps +10.7%, digitally enabled comps +19.5%; August net sales $23.70 billion (+9.9% YoY). Q3 traffic rose only +2.4% (about +5.2% a year earlier), so growth leaned on ticket size. What the market will price is gross margin, core merchandise margin, and expense ratio. Some on the Street argue that stripping out U.S. government tariff refunds could leave core EPS below the $6.53 consensus, making that number closer to a best case.
Focus 3: Tariff refunds, nearly $20 billion in cash, and special-dividend talk
The balance sheet is the other sentiment lever. Cash and equivalents exceed $18.9 billion, with about $1 billion in short-term investments against roughly $5.6 billion of long-term debt. Some estimates put cash near $20 billion and tariff refunds around $1.5 billion. Investors will listen for how management redeploys those refunds — lower prices, new warehouses, or shareholder returns — and whether a special dividend or larger buyback is on the table. A warehouses-only message with no capital-return signal may leave the cash pile inert for the stock.
Focus 4: After the multiple reset, guidance quality decides the bounce
Forward P/E is about 43x, a bit below the five-year average near 45x, but still rich versus high-single- to low-double-digit growth. The average Wall Street target is about $1,085–$1,092, implying roughly 20%+ upside, with a Moderate Buy tilt. Shares dropped about 4% after Q3, a reminder that “in line” is often not enough for COST. Membership, margins, and capital return need to land together.
Risks and Opportunities
Upside catalysts:
Membership-fee growth stays in double digits, U.S./Canada renewals hold near 92%, and Executive memberships keep outpacing the overall base.
EPS reaches or exceeds $6.53 even after stripping one-time tariff items, with core margins better than feared.
A clear special dividend, buyback step-up, or cash-use plan that supports a valuation repair.
Downside risks:
Core EPS misses because of costs, tariffs, or margin pressure, confirming $6.53 as a best-case print.
Traffic keeps slowing and renewals slip as the digital-acquisition mix ages into the renewal calculation.
Vague cash-use commentary and cautious outlook, with high valuation leaving room toward $875 and potentially $844.
Trading Playbook
Bull case: Net sales have already validated share gains. If membership and margins both beat, and management signals a special dividend or buyback, the roughly 18% drawdown can turn into a repair trade.
Bear case: The top line was pre-announced in monthly sales. An EPS “print-and-go,” flat membership metrics, or no capital-return signal can repeat the Q3 pattern: decent results, weaker stock.
Key numbers:
Adjusted EPS and whether tariff refunds or other one-offs are in the figure
Membership-fee income, renewal rates, Executive-member growth
Gross margin / core margin ex-gasoline
Cash, buybacks, special-dividend language; warehouse pipeline and outlook
Tactical notes (as of the September 22 close at $899.41):
Into the print: The stock bounced four sessions off the September 16–21 $885–$896 shelf, tagged $903.40 on September 22, and closed $899.41. It remains below the 10-day MA near $901, 20-day near $919, 50-day near $936, and 200-day near $960 — short- and intermediate-term averages are still stacked bearishly. Price is pinned under the $900 round number into the event; risk/reward is only average. Options imply about a ±3.3%–3.6% move (roughly $868–$932). Keep event size light. Do not add leveraged longs below $885.
Long structure: A close back above $910–$922, with pullbacks holding $900 / $888–$896. Upside references: $936 (50-day) / $960 (200-day). Stops can sit at $885, or below $875 depending on risk tolerance.
Short / hedge structure: A gap that cannot reclaim $888–$896, or a failed push into $910–$922. Downside references: $885 / $875 / $844 (52-week low).
How to use it: If results and capital return both surprise and the stock closes above $910–$922, look for pullbacks toward $900 / $888–$896 rather than chasing the first spike. If the print only confirms already-released sales and margins or membership disappoint, respect the $868–$932 implied range and the $885 / $875 / $844 shelf. Size and stops should match personal risk tolerance.
Disclaimer: For information only. This is not investment advice.
